edges.effect_quant: In comparative meta-analysis, Roux-en-Y gastric bypass carried higher odds of postoperative vitamin B12 deficiency than sleeve gastrectomy (OR 3.55, 95% CI 1.26 to 10.01).
edges.mechanism: Gastric bypass reduces gastric acid exposure, alters intrinsic factor handling, and bypasses proximal gut anatomy involved in normal nutrient processing. Together those changes lower B12 release and uptake, so deficiency can emerge early and persist without structured supplementation.
edges.summary: Vitamin B12 deficiency is a well-established long-term nutritional risk after Roux-en-Y gastric bypass. Prospective biomarker studies, longitudinal micronutrient cohorts, and comparative meta-analysis all point in the same direction: bypass anatomy makes B12 depletion more likely unless patients are monitored and supplemented consistently.
edges.caveats: Risk varies with supplement adherence, baseline stores, type of bypass, and how aggressively deficiency is screened using methylmalonic acid or holotranscobalamin instead of serum B12 alone. This edge is strongest for Roux-en-Y gastric bypass rather than all bariatric procedures as a single group.
